item.title: Small Steps for Coding Agents
item.content:encoded: Coding agents work best when the task is small, the feedback loop is fast and the tests are trustworthy. In this post I describe how I break large changes into reviewable steps, how I write the acceptance criteria before the agent starts, and why I keep the agent away from production credentials. The agent reads the repository, proposes a plan, edits files and runs the test suite after every change. When a test fails, it reads the error output and tries again, and I only step in when the same failure repeats three times. Over a month this workflow shipped forty small pull requests with almost no regressions. The biggest lesson was that a clear definition of done matters more than a clever prompt, because the agent can verify its own work against it without waiting for me.

item.title: What Prompt Caching Taught Me
item.content:encoded: Prompt caching changed how I structure long running tools. Instead of rebuilding the context from scratch on every request, the stable instructions and reference documents go first and the volatile question goes last. That ordering lets the API reuse the cached prefix, which cuts latency and cost for repeated calls. I measured the effect on a documentation assistant that answers hundreds of questions per day against the same manual. Cache reads made the median response noticeably faster, and the monthly bill dropped by more than half. The main pitfall is accidental invalidation: a timestamp or a random identifier near the top of the prompt silently disables the cache. I now add a check in the test suite that fails when the cached prefix changes between two identical requests, so regressions are caught before deployment.

item.title: Static Sites Are Enough
item.content:encoded: Static site generators are a good fit for content that changes only when an editor merges a pull request. Every page is rendered at build time, search engines receive complete HTML, and hosting costs almost nothing. The tradeoff is that interactive features such as filtering and search must run in the browser. For a few thousand articles a prebuilt JSON index is small enough to download once, and libraries designed for static sites can split the search index into chunks that load on demand. I also keep the filter state in the URL query string so that a filtered list can be shared and bookmarked. Progressive enhancement remains important: when JavaScript fails, the category and tag pages still show the full list because they were generated ahead of time.
